ACRT: Autocallable notes tied to the Russell 2000 small-cap index, replicated through an index of staggered weekly notes that pay income and can end early. It is structured income on small-caps: payouts depend on the index staying above set levels, and sharp small-cap drops can cut the notes' value.
ARKE: Exposure to a flagship innovation fund wrapped in a buffer structure for a twelve-month outcome period starting in the third quarter, designed to take part in only half of any loss while capping gains. It layers defense on a volatile growth fund, softening its famous swings.
BAY: Companies based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the region's big technology names plus its banks, health care and consumer firms. It is a hometown concentration bet: one metro area's economy drives it, so a tech downturn or regional shock hits harder than in a national fund.
CBOL: Bitcoin exposure through a ladder of four structured protection funds with staggered outcome periods, built to limit downside while keeping capped upside. It is the laddered sibling in its family: staggering smooths timing risk, though gains still stop at each underlying fund's cap.
CBOT: Companies building robots and humanoid machines for factories, warehouses, hospitals, homes and farms, spread across technology, industrials and consumer names. It is an actively managed bet on embodied AI: the theme is exciting and early, so prices swing on prototypes and promises as much as sales.
CGRO: Growth companies across Greater China: mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, led by consumer firms with industrials and technology behind them. It is an actively managed single-region growth bet: the manager picks high-growth sectors, and Chinese policy swings hit the whole fund at once.
CMAY: S&P 500 exposure through options with a deeper cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. Compared with shallower buffers, it trades a lower cap on gains for protection that covers bigger drops.
COOL: Companies solving the AI data-center heat problem: cooling systems, power management and the electrical gear behind them, split between technology and industrials. It is a picks-and-shovels AI bet on infrastructure nobody sees, swinging with data-center construction rather than software hype.
CRDD: Exposure to Cardano's ADA crypto token through regulated futures contracts, backed by cash and high-quality collateral. It lets traders bet on ADA's price in a brokerage account without holding the token, though futures pricing can drift from spot and crypto swings are large.
CRY: Weekly income from selling options on a leveraged fund tied to Circle, the stablecoin company behind USDC. It stacks options on leverage on one newly public crypto-linked stock, so payouts can be fat but swings are extreme and holding periods should be short.
CTMA: S&P 500 exposure through options with a very deep cushion absorbing the first 30% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. That much protection comes at a price: the cap on gains is low, so it trails badly in strong rallies.
EMMY: Emerging-market stocks through options on an emerging markets fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, and gains capped in exchange. It adds defense to a volatile asset class: EM swings and currency moves still show through.
FLAG: The 50 highest-scoring companies in the S&P 500 on a market leadership ranking, all earning at least half their revenue in the United States, led by technology and health care. It is a concentrated core holding: fifty leaders instead of five hundred, so winners and losers matter more.
FSPC: Companies in the space economy: rocket and satellite makers, launch services and the industrial firms behind them, with industrials about three quarters of the fund. It is a growth bet on space going commercial, concentrated in one young industry that swings with contracts and launch headlines.
HMAY: S&P 500 exposure through options built to protect against all losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange for that full protection. It is the most defensive end of the buffer range: safety is total for the period, but the cap is tight.
IDJN: Developed-market stocks outside North America, in Europe, Japan and similar economies, wrapped in options with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in June. It pairs foreign exposure with defense: gains are capped, and currency moves still play a part.
JULC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in July, with gains capped in exchange. The July start fixes the terms: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap than deeper-protection editions.
KSMH: South Korean companies focused on artificial intelligence semiconductors: the chipmakers and equipment firms producing AI memory and processors. It is a single-country, single-industry bet even narrower than a general chip fund, riding both the AI boom and the Korean market.
LADM: A ladder of twelve monthly buffer funds on the S&P 500, each with moderate protection and its own start date, held in one package. Laddering spreads the timing risk across the year: some protection is always fresh, and no single start date decides the whole outcome.
LBOX: Box spreads, combinations of options that lock in a small, known payoff at expiry, much like lending money until a set date. It is a cash-like parking spot: returns are modest and steady by design, and it deliberately avoids stock market direction altogether.
LIAU: Treasury inflation-protected securities arranged to pay out a stream of income through 2060, with payments that rise alongside consumer prices. It pairs a pension-style payout schedule with inflation protection: the point is dependable real income for decades, not growth.
MAUG: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in August, with gains capped in exchange. It is one edition of a monthly series, and the August start date matters because the protection terms were locked in then.
MAYC: S&P 500 exposure through options with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in May, with gains capped in exchange. The May start fixes the terms: buyers later in the period get whatever protection time remains.
MDCR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in December, with gains capped in exchange. It is the December edition of a monthly series: the year-end start fixes its terms, and later buyers inherit what protection remains.
MFEB: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in February, with gains capped in exchange. It is the February edition of a monthly series: the start month fixes the terms, so identical funds differ only by when their clock began.
MHIP: A strategy built around health care costs, designed to grow faster than medical inflation by combining health-related investments with inflation-sensitive positions. It is a niche hedge holding: the target is beating rising health care bills, so it is judged against medical costs, not the stock market.
MJUN: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in June, with gains capped in exchange. It is the June edition of a monthly series: buying it later means accepting the June terms, not a fresh set of protection.
MMAR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in March, with gains capped in exchange. It is the March edition of a monthly series, chosen by investors who want their protection clock to start in spring.
MNVR: Options on an S&P 500 fund arranged for moderate downside protection over an outcome period that started in November, with gains capped in exchange. It belongs to a monthly series: each edition's protection is set at its own start, so the November terms are the ones that count.
MVAL: Large US companies that Morningstar analysts judge both undervalued and protected by durable competitive advantages, tilted toward consumer staples and health care. It is a value holding with a quality screen: the moat test keeps out cheap-but-fragile firms, though it can lag in growth-led markets.
NICO: Tobacco and nicotine companies worldwide: cigarette makers, vaping and pouch brands, and others earning most of their revenue from nicotine products. It is a deliberately concentrated bet on a controversial industry: these stocks often pay fat dividends, but regulation and lawsuits hang over them permanently.
NRAM: Companies making computer memory: the chip firms that produce the DRAM, flash and next-generation memory AI systems are hungry for. It is a narrow slice of the semiconductor industry, so it swings with memory prices, which are famously cyclical and brutal in downturns.
PCLC: A focused portfolio of large growth companies, with technology over half, picked by a manager looking at businesses from several angles. It is an actively managed growth holding: concentration in tech gives it punch, and bigger swings than a broad index fund.
PHOX: Companies working in photonics and optics: lasers, fiber optics, sensors and the light-based technology inside data centers and medical devices. It is a narrow technology bet on the hardware of the AI buildout, so it swings with data-center spending and chip demand.
QMY: Growth and technology stocks through options on the Nasdaq-100 fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 10% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It is tech growth with a safety net: the shallower buffer leaves a higher cap on gains than deeper versions.
SCMY: Small US companies through options on a small-cap fund, with a cushion absorbing the first 15% of losses over an outcome period that started in May. It adds defense to the market's most volatile tier: small-caps swing hard, so the buffer does real work here.
SCOW: Small US companies with at least seven straight years of positive free cash flow and strong cash returns, spread across technology, financials and consumer stocks. It is a quality screen on the market's smallest tier: the long cash-flow record is the filter, favoring proven survivors over young growers.
TIPD: A ladder of inflation-linked bonds arranged to pay out income through 2055, with payments that adjust as consumer prices rise. It is built for decades-long income plans: the fixed end date sets the schedule, and the inflation link guards purchasing power across a working lifetime.
TSIC: Famous American consumer brands: the food, drink, retail and lifestyle companies that define everyday American life, over half in consumer staples. It is a patriotic-themed core holding: the screen picks iconic names, which tilts it toward familiar household brands rather than the full market.
WTIB: Two commodity bets in one fund: crude oil and bitcoin, both reached through futures contracts and related products. It is a speculative diversifier pairing an old-school commodity with a digital one: both legs are volatile, and futures pricing can add its own drag.
XAIW: Companies in the ecosystem around SpaceX and its AI ventures: launch and satellite suppliers, connectivity firms and the industrials and tech names in their orbit. It is a focused bet built around one private empire's supply chain, so it captures partners rather than the private companies themselves.
XQBT: The ten standout companies in quantum computing, from pure-play quantum firms to big tech names with quantum programs. It is a concentrated bet on an experimental technology: the science is exciting, revenues are small, and prices swing on headlines rather than earnings.
XVAD: AMD shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the chipmaker: the options trade some upside for payouts, and AMD's swings drive everything.
XVAP: Apple shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income on top of following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: Apple drives everything, and the options trade some of its upside for regular payouts.
XVMS: Microsoft shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding: the software giant drives the result, and the options swap some upside for steadier payouts.
XVNV: NVIDIA shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on the AI chip leader: payouts are the goal, but NVIDIA's sharp swings still set the tone.
XVPT: Palantir shares paired with options on the stock, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its price. It is a single-stock income holding on a famously volatile name: the options harvest its swings for payouts, but cannot smooth them away.
XVSP: Shares and options tied to a single private company, SpaceX, arranged to pay a target level of income while following its value. It is a rare way to hold the rocket company in a brokerage account: the income plan is clear, but valuing a private stock makes pricing less certain.
YBTY: A fund of GraniteShares YieldBoost funds, each selling options on leveraged single-stock products to pay high weekly income. It is income squared: layers of options and leverage underneath, diversified across several underlying stocks but with every layer capping gains and adding its own swings.
YYYM: Municipal bond closed-end funds, pooled through an index, which together hold tax-exempt bonds from cities and states across the country. It is a high-income holding: closed-end funds often use leverage and trade at discounts, so payouts run high but prices swing more than plain muni bonds.
